\subsection{Platforms}
\draftnote{Reference fleet (docs/hardware.md): Clearpath Husky with a Velodyne VLP-16 and
RealSense D435i; Tarot 680 hexacopter with a D435i and Cube autopilot (PX4); BlueROV2 with a
Water Linked DVL A50 and Tritech Micron Gemini 720s; quay-side gateway bridging a 5\,GHz Wi-Fi
mesh and Water Linked M64 acoustic modems (64\,bit/s). The BlueROV2 tether never carries
Avatar traffic.}

\subsection{Setup}
\draftnote{Scenarios: Harbor, Dam face, Offshore jacket, Aliasing grid (docs/PLAN.md §6).
Teams: USV+2AUV; UAV+UGV; full. Tier-1 fast simulator; Tier-2 Gazebo Harmonic with
kinematic sensor rigs and a ray-cast sonar proxy (ADR-0007; DAVE and PX4 are future work).
Everything is simulation.}

\subsection{Baselines and metrics}
Independent single-agent SLAM; centralized oracle with ground-truth association; an
\emph{Above-and-Below}-style centralized server~\cite{mcconnell2026aboveandbelow};
Kimera-Multi~\cite{tian2022kimeramulti}, Swarm-SLAM~\cite{lajoie2024swarmslam},
SlideSLAM~\cite{liu2025slideslam} on air/ground subsets; DRACo-SLAM2~\cite{huang2025draco2} on
underwater subsets. Metrics: ATE with 4-DoF alignment~\cite{sturm2012tum, umeyama1991}, team ATE
in a common frame, frame error, association precision, bytes per link type.

\subsection{Results}
\draftnote{Tier-1 simulation, except the Tier-2 paragraph. Numbers are regenerated by
\texttt{make -C experiments paper-data} (Tier 2: \texttt{tier2}); tables are
\texttt{\textbackslash input} from \texttt{paper/data/}.}

Table~\ref{tab:server} compares \avatar{} with an \emph{Above-and-Below}-style centralized
server~\cite{mcconnell2026aboveandbelow} that receives the robots' keyframes (odometry and
detections) over the same links and budgets, runs the same association front-end and cycle
check, and solves one joint graph. The downlink is not charged, which favors the server.
With ideal links, the server matches the oracle, so any gap comes from the bytes and not from
the estimator. On acoustic links of 64--100\,bit/s the keyframe stream cannot keep up, and the
server rarely merges the AUVs, whereas \avatar{}'s condensed landmarks bring the whole team into
one frame in every run. At 1\,kbit/s the stream keeps up: the server merges the team, later
than \avatar{} and with slightly larger error. The server's failure case is instructive: with a small
fraction of an AUV's keyframes it can accept an aliased AUV--AUV alignment that no cycle vetoes,
which produces the large error at 100\,bit/s.

\paragraph{Correcting a drifting AUV}
\IfFileExists{data/drift_summary.tex}{\input{data/drift_summary.tex}}{\newcommand{\driftSmallRuns}{?}\newcommand{\driftSmallMeanChange}{?}}
We claim collaboration only for small drift (Table~\ref{tab:drift}). A BlueROV2 makes a
one-way transit through the sparse outer harbor, and both ends of the transit lie in water
that another AUV surveys. Over the \driftSmallRuns{} runs whose solo drift stays below 1\,m,
sharing changes the drifting vehicle's error by \driftSmallMeanChange\,\% on average. The gain
is not uniform: some runs improve substantially, and a few get slightly worse. Metre-level
drift is not yet corrected (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Perception in Gazebo (Tier 2)}
\IfFileExists{data/tier2_summary.tex}{\input{data/tier2_summary.tex}}{%
  \providecommand{\tierOneAvatar}{?}\providecommand{\tierOneOracle}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoAvatar}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoOracle}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoWrong}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoGOne}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoMerged}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoRuns}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoNNGOne}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoNNWrong}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoNNAvatar}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoRegGOne}{?}%
  \providecommand{\tierTwoNNUuvGOne}{?}\providecommand{\tierTwoNNLandGOne}{?}}
The same scenario is rendered in Gazebo Harmonic. Each robot is a kinematic sensor rig placed at
its ground-truth pose at every keyframe, with a VLP-16, a D435i depth camera, and a ray-cast
proxy for the imaging sonar (no speckle, multipath, or shadows). Odometry, depth, and ground
truth are those of Tier 1 for the same seed, so only perception differs. A geometric front-end
gates returns by medium, removes ground and seabed, clusters, and fits circles. Extended objects
such as hulls have no viewpoint-invariant centre and are mostly dropped. Table~\ref{tab:tier2} reports
\tierTwoRuns{} seeds. With ground-truth intra-agent tracks, the team merges in every run
(\tierTwoMerged), no accepted alignment is wrong (\tierTwoWrong{} wrong), and the frame error of
every robot stays below 1\,m (gate G1, \tierTwoGOne{} runs). Team ATE is \tierTwoAvatar\,m against
\tierTwoOracle\,m for the oracle, versus \tierOneAvatar\,m and \tierOneOracle\,m in Tier 1: the
ratio to the oracle is similar, and the absolute error grows because noisy clusters replace idealized
detections. This does not yet show that G1 holds on realistic sonar images, since the proxy is
idealized.

A nearest-neighbour tracker that associates detections in the dead-reckoning frame is not
sufficient. G1 holds in only \tierTwoNNGOne{} runs, with \tierTwoNNWrong{} wrong alignments and
a team ATE of \tierTwoNNAvatar\,m; registering each keyframe to the track map first is worse
(G1 in \tierTwoRegGOne{} runs). The failure is mostly underwater (Table~\ref{tab:tier2agents}): with
this tracker on the BlueROV2s alone G1 holds in \tierTwoNNUuvGOne{} runs, on the Husky and Tarot
alone in \tierTwoNNLandGOne{}. A BlueROV2's raw dead-reckoning drift becomes comparable to the
spacing of similar piles, so the gate cannot tell them apart. Association has to use the agent's
own estimate (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}); the ground-truth-track row is therefore the
result for the estimator, and the two tracker rows are negative results for the front-end.

\subsection{Ablations}
\paragraph{Acoustic rate and digest order}
Table~\ref{tab:bandwidth} sweeps the raw modem rate (shared by the three acoustic nodes) for
three digest orders. Below a few tens of bit/s the team cannot merge within the mission. From
64\,bit/s up, the link budget, not the order, sets when frames connect.

\paragraph{Front-end errors}
Table~\ref{tab:realism} injects identity switches (a detection attributed to a nearby part of
the same medium) and clutter into every agent's front-end. Without a robust kernel the team
falls apart; a Huber kernel limits the damage; graduated non-convexity keeps every agent,
and the team, at its error-free accuracy. The oracle keeps ground-truth association and is
not shown.
